title: A few months ago, I wondered what it was like opening the b
text:
A few months ago, I wondered what it was like opening the box.
Radio represents a huge portion of the media broadcasting landscape in the United States. Though it often takes backseat to TV and Internet in the public eye, radio reaches an estimated 271 million Americans weekly. That translates to approximately $22 billion in revenues (about 14% of the $148 billion broadcasting market in 2015, according to Statista ). Similarly, the SNL Kagan estimates that in 2017 the radio industry will generate $17.8 billion just in advertising revenue.
With such a large revenue pie, naturally we begin to wonder just how competitive the industry is, who will complete for a slice, and when (not if) the industry will become completely digital-dependent through technology, online streaming, satellite, and the like. That said, Pandora ( P ), Sirius ( SIRI ), Entercom ( ETM ), iHeartRadio ( OTCPK:IHRT ), and Cumulus ( CMLS ) are all players in the radio-online audio business (not to mention Spotify ( MUSIC ) and Apple Music ( AAPL )).
Interestingly, when comparing these companies against price/sales and EV/Sales ratios, it turns out that Pandora is the most undervalued of the bunch, despite never turning a profit in its six-year history as a publicly traded company. Although Pandora has shown declines in both active listeners and total listener hours over the last two years, new CEO Roger Lynch will take Pandora management to task, and work to improve content, distribution, listener addition & retention, and market execution. Through relative valuation, investigating the executive strategy under new CEO Roger Lynch, and comparing industry players, we will see that Pandora shares can be reasonably valued at $10.65 per share, representing approximately 100% upside.
